glossary.definition: A Ping release claim (2026-11-02), listing and cap measured on gateway v1.261106 (2026-11-08), access by caller measured per aggregate (2026-11-09), per-tool filtering per caller UNVERIFIED on our tenant, and simulated in this app: an aggregate of member MCP servers has one policy that caps what any member tool may be used for. It is enforced on the listing and again at the member hop. The cap only removes: a tool the member itself denies stays denied. The console API has no field for it, so this lab gives it no field name.

Characters that take no space or change the order text is drawn in (bidirectional controls, zero-width spaces, Unicode tag characters). They let a description show one thing to a person and say another to a model. The scanner reports them with each character shown as [U+XXXX].

The step before a tool call is sent: the tool shows the exact arguments and a hash of them, and refuses the call without an explicit confirm that carries that hash. It guards against a click you did not mean and against changed arguments.

A Ping release claim (2026-11-02), listing and cap measured on gateway v1.261106 (2026-11-08), access by caller measured per aggregate (2026-11-09), per-tool filtering per caller UNVERIFIED on our tenant, and simulated in this app: a tool the caller is not entitled to is removed from tools/list instead of only being refused when called, and it is refused again when called by name. The simulation is lab-invented; the console API has no field for it.
A tool parameter whose default points off-box (a callback URL or an email address). An agent that fills arguments from the schema sends data there on every call.

A scan of an entitlement-filtered list covers only what that caller sees. A tool hidden from this caller was never scanned, so a clean result is not a clean result for any other caller. The scan notes and the Limits page say so.
Text in tool metadata written for the model rather than the person: an instruction tag, an order to keep something from the user, or an imperative aimed at the agent.
The part of this tool that connects to an MCP server and shows what it offers (tools, resources, prompts) as plain text, and can call a tool after a confirm step. It sees; it does not judge.

A local debugging passthrough in this app. Point an MCP client at it instead of at the server and every JSON-RPC message it sends and gets back is logged, with timing and an estimated token cost. It enforces no policy and the confirm step does not cover the agent's calls through it; it is not a gateway.

An application of type mcp-aggregate that merges several member MCP servers into one. Console swagger names, 2026-10-31, schema only: Members, and per member AppRef, Alias and ToolFilter. The schema says a member's tools are namespaced as Alias__tool. These names already existed on 2026-10-26; the behaviour is a Ping claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.
A tool whose name equals, or looks like, a tool you already trust from another server, so an agent that resolves tools by name may pick the wrong one.

A Markdown file this app builds from the items an operator flagged on a server: the notes, the server's own definitions and the scan findings, for a coding agent or a reviewer. Server text is fenced and labelled as untrusted data, so the brief does not pass on the injection it reports.

The machine-readable result of a scan (scan-report/1): the findings with rule id, severity and evidence, the input counts, the rule table and the list of what a metadata scan cannot catch. It records enforcement as none.

How much of an agent's context a tool list, a definition or a result takes up, estimated as characters divided by four. It is a rough rule, not a tokenizer: real counts differ by model. A long or poisoned tool list costs the agent context before it does anything.

Console swagger name, 2026-10-31, schema only: a string array on each aggregate member. The schema gives the name and type and nothing about meaning. This lab reads it as the allow-list of that member's tools the aggregate exposes; that reading is the lab's.
What a server says about its tools: names, descriptions and input schemas. An agent reads it as trusted context before it ever calls a tool.
Putting instructions or traps in tool metadata. The model reads that text as trusted context and the person normally never sees it.

Accepting whatever a server presents the first time and noticing only later changes. It is safe only if the first presentation was vetted. A scan before first use is that vetting; a scan is one list at one moment.

glossary.term: Why it matters: MCP aggregate (Ping claims)
glossary.definition: Ping claims from its H2 2026 deck (slide 37), UNVERIFIED on our tenant. Challenge: each agent-server pair needs its own connection, configuration and credential, so effort and attack surface grow with each pair. Technical: one connection, one policy cap enforced twice, one audit trail across members. Business: new servers join by configuration, not project work, for a lower per-integration cost and a faster rollout.

glossary.term: Why it matters: MCP gateway (Ping claims)
glossary.definition: Ping claims from its H2 2026 deck (slide 36), UNVERIFIED on our tenant. Challenge: one shared token and every tool exposed to every caller means no attribution and no per-tool control, so security stalls adoption. Technical: per-user identity, per-tool policy and injected credentials on every call, fully audited. Business: MCP integrations proceed under existing governance, with faster time to value on agent projects.
